    Kiwi Ears Stardust Review

    Marcelo
    IEM & Earphones
    November 4, 2026
    Listen to audio version of this article
    Sponsored by
    0:00 / 8:20
    Instaread

    Marcelo reviews the Kiwi Ears Stardust, an affordable hybrid in-ear monitor featuring a custom 10mm PU+LCP dynamic driver with four BA drivers. Its SRP is $76.99 for the standard 3.5mm cable option, but it is currently on promotion at $65.44 for 11:11.

    Disclaimer: This sample was sent in exchange for my honest opinion. Headfonics is an independent website with no affiliate links or services. I thank Linsoul and Kiwi Ears for their support.

    Click here to read up on the Kiwi Ears gear previously reviewed on Headfonics.

    This article follows our scoring guidelines, which you can read in more detail here.

    Kiwi Ears Stardust Review
    Summary
    Thanks to the 1DD+4BA hybrid driver configuration, even at high volume and with complex music, the Kiwi Ears Stardust IEM stayed composed, rendering the music with reasonable clarity and separation, which I find remarkable for its price.

    Kiwi Ears

    Have you ever wished IEM makers engineered affordable IEM sets so that nearly all the budget went into making the sound quality as good as possible? With as little as possible going into accessories?

    That thought came to mind when I read about the Kiwi Ears Stardust, a 1DD+4BA hybrid driver configuration that sells for $76.99 to $79.99, depending on the cable option.

    I have reviewed other hybrids in this price range, including the FiiO SNOWSKY FH3 LUMI, FiiO JadeAudio JH13, and the TinHIFI T6, and none have nearly as many drivers as the Kiwi Ears Stardust.

    You see, I’m wary of products that promise too much but underdeliver, and I think the high driver count for the price of the Kiwi Ears Stardust is promising too much.

    Will the Kiwi Ears Stardust deliver a good or a disappointing sound? How will it compare to the LUMI, the Hidizs MS2 PRO, and the TinHIFI T6? Let’s find out.

    Features

    The Kiwi Ears Stardust features a 1DD+4BA hybrid driver configuration, with a custom 10mm PU+LCP dynamic driver for the bass and midrange frequencies and four balanced armature drivers for the highs and ultra-highs.

    Ultra-budget brands with poor quality control and bad sound quality offer the same driver count. But it is rare to find this driver count at this price point in an IEM from a highly reputed brand for its sound quality, such as Kiwi Ears.

    The Stardust has an average sensitivity of 107 dB/mW and an impedance of 13Ω, which is quite low.

    Design

    Aside from the metal ring around the faceplate, Stardust’s construction and design are typical of a budget, entry-level model. Stardust features an all-3D-printed resin shell, nozzle, and faceplate, and terminates with a 2-pin connection. 

    Still, the Stardust’s hand-assembled shell doesn’t look or feel entry-level or cheap. From afar, it looks like a gem; the embedded green faceplate graphics are designed to look layered, giving an illusion of 3-dimensionality.

    A stainless grill covers the 6.5mm diameter nozzle. The Stardust weighs only 4.4 grams, which is very light.

    Stock Cable

    I’m grateful Kiwi Ears didn’t totally cheap out on the cable for the Stardust.

    The dual-core, silver-plated OFC cable may not look or feel luxurious, but it is a league above most budget or entry-level IEMs in quality, thanks to its thickness and metal parts.

    At checkout, you can choose from three cable options: a 3.5mm with no mic, a 3.5mm with mic, and a USB-C with mic.

    Comfort & Isolation

    The Stardust’s lightweight, ergonomic shape makes it comfortable for long walks or casual listening at home. No part of the shell presses on my ears, and the pressure relief prevents discomfort from buildup in my ear canal.

    The noise isolation is average, which I actually like because I still want to hear what’s happening around me when I stop the music.

    Packaging & Accessories

    The Stardust came in a decent-looking, well-protected green box with a photo of the Stardust on the front and text all around.

    It measures 126 x 106 x 37 mm and contains the pair of Stardust IEMs, a 3.5mm cable, a manual, a carrying case, and six pairs of ear tips.

    Sound Impressions

    I did my standard 24-hour burn-in just to let the drivers settle and used the stock black ear tips and 3.5mm stock cable for listening and comparison.

    For the sources, I used my MUSE HiFi M3 Ultra, xDuoo XP-2 Bal DAC amplifiers, my Android phone, and the FiiO M15S DAP, using YouTube Music, UAPP, or PowerAmp. I did not use EQ or sound-enhancement programs and listened at medium-to-loud volumes.

    Measurements

    My Stardust measurements reveal a basically perfectly channel-matched set, indicating high production quality.

    This is impressive given its driver count and price. The blunt peak around 8kHz is audible but gentle, as is the mild upper-midrange elevation.

    Summary

    Reading through the Stardust’s product page, I get the impression that it is tuned near neutral with a moderate sub-bass boost, and indeed it is.

    The Stardust has a moderate sub-bass boost, a near-neutral, moderately V-shaped sound signature, and a well-balanced tonality.

    The bass is only moderately boosted, so I need a bassy track to hear the boost, since it is near-neutral with a fast, tight character. Luckily, thanks to its sub-bass boost, the bass never sounds thin and lightweight.

    The boost is mostly in the sub-bass, so most 80s and 90s pop songs or similarly mixed songs are not affected, only modern music where there is more sub-bass content in the track.

    I like that the mid-bass/lower midrange isn’t recessed as in other IEMs tuned for a deliberate sub-bass boost, which I don’t like. The Stardust’s mid-bass and lower midrange sound natural and avoid thinning the vocal note weight.

    Thanks to the good mid-bass/lower midrange tuning, and even with the moderate upper midrange elevation, the Stardust sounds very balanced in the vocals and midrange.

    The Stardust’s treble is remarkably clean, smooth, and extended for a hybrid IEM in its price range, and it’s never harsh or sharp like most hybrid IEMs I’ve heard in this range. There is a reasonable amount of detail and air.

    Coloration

    As mentioned above, the Stardust is remarkably clean for the price and has good clarity and detail. I hear no bass coloration at all, even with its moderate boost, as it only adds a little excitement and life to the music.

    However, I can clearly hear an elevation in the upper midrange around 2kHz; though it isn’t shouty or peaky, it sounds a little too energetic and lively in that frequency.

    And though it never sounds nasal, even on relaxed music, I can always hear forwardness in the upper midrange coloring the sound.

    Additionally, there is a moderately perceivable peak around 8kHz, which is mild and never sounds sharp. Still, it adds extra treble energy and, due to its elevation, seems to mask the frequencies above it, even though I can still hear some upper-treble detail and energy.

    Though my description might make the Stardust sound peaky and fatiguing, I never find it fatiguing.

    Those frequency-response deviations are mild enough not to cause fatigue, but they add excitement, life, and a little coloration; Stardust sounds clean and never distorted.

    Soundstage & Dynamics

    Though it doesn’t have the biggest soundstage I’ve heard, the Stardust is on the more spacious side of average among the competing IEMs I’ve heard recently. I never felt the Stardust’s soundstage sounded cramped; it always has notable spaciousness.

    The soundstage doesn’t have much height, though, and it’s wider than it is deep. I’m judging the Stardust based on all the IEMs I’ve heard and my standards, but for the price, I have no right to complain, as the soundstage is almost as good as it gets in this price range.

    Imaging is reasonably good, with distinct image placement, edge definition, and noticeable side-to-side spatial separation.

    It’s not the best imaging performance I’ve heard, though, as it lacks the palpability and see-through transparency, as you can almost see the singer in front.

    Dynamically, the Stardust is excellent. I like how it renders sound with bubbling energy; the bass is fast and weighty when needed, the midrange is energetic, and the treble has good excitement.

    Like many IEMs I’ve heard in recent years, the Stardust has no problem getting very loud and staying clean when fed high amplifier power.
